title: Machiavelli: Realism, Statecraft, and Secular Politics

scenes.text: Should a ruler be loved or feared to keep a nation secure?
scenes.narration: Imagine you are running a country surrounded by rivals. Would you rule by winning people's love, or by making them fear your power?

scenes.text: A strict school monitor enforcing order instead of trying to be everyone's favorite friend.
scenes.narration: Here's an analogy to make this click: think of your school monitor. If they only try to be popular, the classroom turns into chaos, but firm rules keep everyone safe and disciplined.

scenes.name: Niccolò Machiavelli
scenes.idea: Studied politics as a realistic power struggle rather than an imagined moral ideal.
scenes.narration: Scholar Harold Laski called Machiavelli a child of the Renaissance. Writing in divided Italy, he rejected religious dogmas to pioneer realism, observing politics as it really is, not how it ought to be.

scenes.heading: Realistic View of Human Nature
items: Ungrateful and quick to forget past favors
Deceitful and ready to betray for self-interest
Cowardly and constantly driven by fear of loss
Avaricious and fiercely protective of personal property
scenes.narration: Machiavelli argued that human nature never changes. Since people are naturally ungrateful, deceitful, cowardly, and greedy, a wise prince controls them through fear rather than trusting in their love.

scenes.heading: Statecraft: The Fox and Lion

columns.title: The Fox
items: Clever enough to recognize hidden traps
Relies on sharp intelligence and foresight

columns.title: The Lion
items: Brave enough to fight off wolves
Commands defense forces and hard power

scenes.narration: To rule successfully, a prince must combine two beasts. You need the cleverness of a fox to spot hidden conspiracies, and the courage of a lion to terrify powerful enemies.

scenes.heading: Dual Morality in Politics
scenes.narration: Here is Machiavelli's big breakthrough: dual morality. While an ordinary person may sacrifice life for private principles, a ruler's highest moral duty is national interest, where the ends justify the means.

items: Political realism: see power as it really is
Statecraft requires both fox cunning and lion bravery
Dual morality places national interest above private ethics
scenes.narration: Remember these three big ideas for your exam: see politics realistically, combine the fox with the lion, and judge political decisions strictly by national survival.
